cases.title: Staffing a desk that verifies affair disclosures
cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in a company statement dated 8 November 2026.
scenario: The public statement is the factual anchor only. Every person, household, provider, transaction, response and number in this case is fictional and is not a description of Huang, his family or any observed consequence of the statement.

A fictional reporting desk sells standardized, verified summaries of public affair disclosures to subscribing publishers. It checks public statements, not private lives. Publishers are assumed to purchase all output at the stated price. The desk chooses verification-worker hours and archive equipment to meet this service demand; each part specifies a distinct change in its workflow, client price, staff cost or available hours.

Its production is Y=A√(KN), where Y is verified-summary output, K is installed archive/editing equipment and N is verification-worker hours. Baseline A=4, K=25, output price P=1 and nominal hourly wage W=5, so w=W/P=5 is the labor cost measured in summary output units, not a consumer-price-index wage.

The desk is a price taker. Inputs and output are divisible; there are no hiring costs. Installed K is fixed when N is chosen, except where a part asks for an earlier capacity plan. Capital receives MPK when both factor payments are requested. Every part resets as stated.

The quantities, prices and technology changes are teaching calibrations. A request for more reporting, a different verification workflow or a particular price response is stipulated where used; nothing here estimates a public figure’s effect on output or employment.
objectives: Derive hiring from MPN=w and separate movements from shifts.
Reconcile factor payments, real and nominal magnitudes, and capital stocks.
Test inverse inferences and a capacity/shutdown boundary.
cases.focus: Production, real wages and capacity

scenario: The public statement is the factual anchor only. Every person, household, provider, transaction, response and number in this case is fictional and is not a description of Huang, his family or any observed consequence of the statement.

A fictional adult is deciding how much paid administrative work to accept at an affair-recovery counselling centre after an affair in their own fictional household. They also value nonwork time for rest and voluntary counselling. The model does not measure emotional harm: leisure l is all discretionary nonwork time, and its utility weight is a stated assumption.

After fixed commitments, h=12 hours remain. Paid hours are N=12−l. Preferences are U=ln c+2ln l, with c>0 and 0<l≤12; the real budget is c=w(12−l)+m. Baseline w=3 and m=18, a support grant available independently of work. The grant is spendable on consumption and is not a wage subsidy.

Higher offered wages represent the centre bidding for administrative hours as its stipulated counselling caseload rises. Grant changes represent alternative assistance arrangements. Other job conditions, available time and preferences remain fixed unless stated; the cases do not infer these changes from the public news.

Part F introduces another adult with a mandatory counselling-related consumption floor of 30: c is total consumption spending, c−30 is the discretionary component, and utility is ln(c−30)+2ln l. The first adult has no such floor. Parts G and H separately examine grant design and identification. Hicks compensation is a model utility benchmark, not a claim that money removes personal harm.
objectives: Check feasible endpoints before applying a tangency.
Derive labor supply and evaluate positive, zero and opposing effects.
Separate Hicks compensation from actual income and aggregate heterogeneous workers.

cases.title: Scheduling recovery bills and ordinary consumption
cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in a company statement dated 8 November 2026.
scenario: The public statement is the factual anchor only. Every person, household, provider, transaction, response and number in this case is fictional and is not a description of Huang, his family or any observed consequence of the statement.

After an affair in a fictional household, the adults choose temporary separate living and counselling. One household member must fund a fixed package of those costs and decide how much ordinary consumption to retain at two dates. The required package is already specified; this model does not choose counselling quality or value relationship outcomes.

Let y₁=120 and y₂=80 be resources available after the required housing and counselling bills have been paid. Thus c₁ and c₂ are ordinary discretionary consumption, excluding those bills. A bill waiver raises the corresponding y; an extra required bill lowers it. Baseline assets and terminal bequests are zero.

The person can borrow or lend through a hypothetical recovery budget account at the same gross real return R=2. U=√c₁+β√c₂ with β=1/2, unless a part infers the parameters. All consumption is nonnegative. The large returns in the exercises are teaching calibrations, not available financial products or advice.

Saving after the required bills is s₁=y₁−c₁ and c₂=y₂+Rs₁. Each part resets as stated and specifies which bill, reimbursement timing or account return changes. All dated bills and resources are certain in the model; unrestricted borrowing is maintained throughout this case.
objectives: Derive the Euler-budget solution and recognize rising, falling and flat profiles.
Keep current and future goods separate in MPCs and wealth comparisons.
Use observed allocations and responses to test whether one model can explain all evidence.
cases.focus: Consumption smoothing and dated responses

cases.title: Separate finances, immediate bills and credit limits
cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in a company statement dated 8 November 2026.
scenario: The public statement is the factual anchor only. Every person, household, provider, transaction, response and number in this case is fictional and is not a description of Huang, his family or any observed consequence of the statement.

Following an affair in a fictional household, an adult chooses to manage finances separately and must pay specified current housing and counselling bills. Their usable resources after these required bills are y₁=60 now and y₂=150 later. Ordinary consumption c excludes the fixed required bills. No initial assets or bequests are present.

The adult no longer uses a joint credit facility by the scenario’s explicit agreement. A new individual facility may allow borrowing up to B. This is a stipulated contract, not a rule that affairs automatically remove credit. Preferences are U=ln c₁+.8ln c₂, both consumptions are positive, and the common borrowing/lending gross real return is R=1.25.
Saving is s=y₁−c₁ and c₂=y₂+1.25s. Lending is unrestricted; borrowing is s≥−B, equivalent to c₁≤y₁+B. B=0 means no borrowing. A loan adds cash access, not lifetime wealth.

Where a provider postpones x of the required current bill, it charges 1.25x later: available resources become (60+x, 150−1.25x). This is a bill-timing arrangement that preserves present wealth while altering cash access. Other parts specify bill waivers, extra future bills, or a voluntary support transfer between two fictional households. Each reset is explicit.
objectives: Compare an unconstrained optimum with the credit ceiling before using Euler equality.
Identify thresholds, positive and zero wedges, and piecewise responses.
Explain why equal present wealth need not imply equal consumption under credit limits.
cases.focus: Credit limits and changing regimes

cases.title: A recovery reserve: cash, wealth and asset timing
cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in a company statement dated 8 November 2026.
scenario: The public statement is the factual anchor only. Every person, household, provider, transaction, response and number in this case is fictional and is not a description of Huang, his family or any observed consequence of the statement.

A fictional adult maintains a financial reserve for temporary separate living and counselling after an affair in their household. The reserve has gross financial assets 90 and debt 65, so net assets are 25. Some assets are equity in an unrelated fictional publisher of affair-recovery workbooks. Stated booking/order revisions change the market value of that holding; the numerical revaluations are given, not derived from public news or personal conduct.

Parts A and B ask whether arranging cash and paying down this reserve’s debt create wealth. Parts C–H reset to the adult’s two-period consumption plan after fixed housing and counselling bills. Available non-asset incomes are y₁=50, y₂=100; preferences are U=ln c₁+.5ln c₂ and baseline gross real return R=2. These are hypothetical teaching units and returns.

In C–H, a₀ denotes the entire net reserve entering the interest period. It earns R before period-1 consumption, following Supplement 3A. Any stated equity revaluation changes a₀ before that interest period. After that, remaining assets and debt are treated as one liquid net position earning the same R, with no further price risk.

Except where a part prohibits debt, borrowing and lending are unrestricted. Closing net assets are a₁=Ra₀+y₁−c₁; saving during the interest period is s₁=a₁−a₀=y₁+(R−1)a₀−c₁. Pre-period revaluations are not saving during this period. There are no terminal bequests. Every shock and reset is stated; personal reserve outcomes are not aggregate wealth or GDP estimates.
objectives: Separate a balance-sheet revaluation, financing transaction and saving flow.
Analyze explicit asset gains and losses with and without borrowing.
Test whether present-value compensation and local rate neutrality survive boundaries and finite changes.
cases.focus: Wealth, saving flows and initial-asset timing

cases.title: An affair disclosure, counselling time and paid work
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All people, relationships, businesses, transactions and economic outcomes in this case are fictional. The scenario is not about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to his acknowledgement. Every numerical assumption is stipulated for the EC2102 exercise.

An affair has been disclosed within a fictional household. Mira wants time away from paid work for counselling and household coordination while financing her own consumption. Let lₜ denote valued nonwork time, which may include those activities. It is chosen, not a compulsory minimum. The exercise models budget and time choices, not the psychological effects of an affair.
Mira chooses c₁,c₂,l₁,l₂ with U=ln c₁+ln l₁+0.5(ln c₂+ln l₂). Each date has h=12 hours, 0<lₜ≤12 and cₜ>0. Paid work is nₜ=12−lₜ. The preference weights are fixed in every comparison.

Her initial current flexible-work offer pays w₁=2; a confirmed later offer pays w₂=6. Baseline R=2, no initial assets, no other income or charges, and unrestricted borrowing/lending at the same R. The high return is a teaching calibration. No terminal financial assets remain.

Dated budgets are c₁+s₁=w₁n₁+b−F₁ and c₂=w₂n₂+Rs₁. A part may add a fixed current contribution F₁ toward separate-living expenses, replace it with an earnings-linked contribution that lowers the net wage, or give an outside relative’s liquid grant b. Otherwise F₁=b=0. These contributions go outside Mira’s own budget; she receives no refund or future offset. Grants require no repayment.

Each part states the concrete change in the work offer, financing rule or support arrangement and resets the other parameters. The contribution experiments use the same budget effects as the course’s lump-sum and proportional-earnings charges. They are hypothetical private arrangements, not statements about legal obligations.
objectives: Derive paid work, nonwork time and consumption jointly when an affair-related household adjustment requires financing.
Distinguish a time boundary from a bank-borrowing boundary.
Compare fixed expense contributions, earnings-linked contributions and outside support.

cases.title: Paying for counselling and separate living
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All people, relationships, businesses, transactions and economic outcomes in this case are fictional. The scenario is not about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to his acknowledgement. Every numerical assumption is stipulated for the EC2102 exercise.

A fictional household has already chosen counselling and a separate-living arrangement after an affair disclosure. The service path is fixed within each comparison. The questions concern how its real resource cost and payment dates affect discretionary consumption; they do not assess whether the services are desirable.

For A–E the household earns Y₁=Y₂=400, has no initial net assets, and chooses discretionary consumption with U=ln C₁+ln C₂. The gross real return is R=1, with unrestricted borrowing and lending. Its required service costs are initially E₁=E₂=100. There are no terminal assets or debts.

It uses a dedicated expense account. Transfers from its main account are initially T₁=T₂=100. The expense account pays Eₜ and may borrow or save at R=1. T₁+T₂=E₁+E₂ ensures no terminal debt. The transfers are internal bookkeeping, not taxes and not an additional resource cost.

Main-account saving is Y₁−T₁−C₁. Expense-account saving is T₁−E₁. Consolidated household saving is their sum, Y₁−C₁−E₁. Initially C₁=C₂=300 and all three balances are zero. These are one household’s balances, not national saving or GDP.

F–H use a different household A with gross income 160 at each date, no assets, U=ln c₁+0.5ln c₂ and R=1. Its current counselling/separate-living bill is 120, with no new bill next date, so its original resources after payments are (40,160). It cannot take a bank loan. Its provider can nevertheless explicitly permit fee deferral q between 0 and 120, repaid next date without interest. Liquid saving s₁≥0 is distinct from this permitted provider debt q.

Thus F–G have c₁+s₁=40+q and c₂=160−q+s₁. The date-1 net financial position after provider debt is s₁−q. Part H explicitly moves the deferred obligation to a different household B; do not treat an outside transfer as merely rescheduling A’s own bill.
objectives: Consolidate internal account transfers so the same expense is counted once.
Compare current, future and repeated service-cost increases with equal-present-value payment timing.
Separate liquid saving from provider debt and trace which household ultimately bears a deferred bill.
cases.focus: A household expense account, provider credit and the incidence of outside support

A fictional counselling service supplies appointments to households dealing with affair disclosures. It decides how many staff hours to hire and how much consultation-room equipment to install. Output below is real service revenue at normalized fixed selling prices, not a count of affairs or a measure of social welfare.

Its two-period plan begins with K₁=50, depreciation d=0.2 and gross return R=1.2. New room capital J≥0 costs 2 per unit now; K₂=40+J. There is no date-1 buyer for inherited survivors, so the service cannot sell them at that date.

Baseline present-value profit is Π=12√N₁−3N₁−2J+[20√K₂+12√N₂−3N₂+1.6K₂]/1.2. The 1.6K₂ term is terminal resale, already net of physical depreciation. Staff hours are freely hired at the stated wages. All choices are nonnegative.

Parts C,D,H examine a referral network that takes a share τ of all date-2 service revenue, with no deduction for labor or room costs and no claim on equipment resale. Its retained-revenue equation is identical to the lecture’s output-revenue-tax wedge. The stated technology and client opportunities are held fixed when isolating this fee effect.

The other parts change a recruitment wage, a specified confidentiality protocol that reduces room-capital productivity, or a physical limit on confidential consultation space. These changes are explicitly part of the hypothetical service arrangement, not effects inferred from a real person’s conduct. Reset to the stated baseline in each comparison.
objectives: Value staff hours and new room capital at the correct dates.
Apply a proportional referral-revenue wedge without confusing it with a tax on profit.
Check zero investment, room-capacity constraints and identical stocks with different marginal incentives.

cases.title: Equipment contracts for public affair-news coverage
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All people, relationships, businesses, transactions and economic outcomes in this case are fictional. The scenario is not about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to his acknowledgement. Every numerical assumption is stipulated for the EC2102 exercise.

A fictional publisher produces explanatory coverage of public affair acknowledgements. It uses published statements and voluntary interviews; this is not a private-investigation scenario. It must decide how much recording equipment to buy now for next period’s coverage and how to value syndication and equipment contracts.

Its two-period equipment model has K₁=64, depreciation d=0.25, survivors 48, R=1.25 and additions J≥0. Capital is the only variable input. Future real content revenue is 24√K₂, so its marginal revenue product is 12/√K₂ and K₂=48+J. Demand and the revenue function are fixed unless stated.

Current equipment price is q₁=8. A dealer’s baseline terminal buyback price is q₂=8 per surviving unit. At date 2 the publisher sells (1−d)K₂. Borrowing is unrestricted. A part may explicitly permit selling date-1 survivors at the same current purchase price.

A syndicator may retain a share τ of future content revenue, but receives none of equipment resale. A dealer or syndicator may offer an immediate credit z per newly purchased unit. These private contract terms create the same marginal equations as the lecture’s revenue tax and investment credit. Baseline τ=z=0; they are not an actual government response to an affair.

Use Π=−(8−z)J+[(1−τ)24√K₂+0.75q₂K₂]/1.25, apart from fixed profits. A particular part separately compares an immediate equipment credit with a hypothetical usable future tax deduction. All stated tax treatment is an exercise assumption, not current tax guidance.

Dealer buyback offers and capacity conditions are explicit counterfactual contracts. If an uncapped resale commitment creates an unbounded model, identify that failure instead of claiming a real publisher can earn unlimited profit.
objectives: Translate recording-equipment contract terms into dated user cost.
Separate investment incentives from the total cost of a revenue-sharing contract.
Test irreversibility, exact break-even values and the need for a cap on a resale offer.

cases.title: Liquid cash and bonds for an affair-related household transition
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All people, relationships, businesses, transactions and economic outcomes in this case are fictional. The scenario is not about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to his acknowledgement. Every numerical assumption is stipulated for the EC2102 exercise.

After an affair disclosure within a fictional household, one member must fund counselling and separate-living bills from an independently managed account. Some bills need immediate cash, while resources left over can earn a nominal return. The exercise uses a stipulated household demand for liquid balances to compare that liquidity need with the opportunity cost of cash.

For the cash-planning parts, real household income is Y=600, the real comparison return is r=0.04 and expected growth of its consumption-price index is πᵉ=0.02 initially. Cash pays zero interest. Its desired real cash reserve is L=400+0.5Y−2000i+D, where D is extra liquidity demand associated with upfront transition bills or uncertain access to shared funds. Initially D=0.

Use the course approximation i=r+πᵉ in this stipulated cash-demand model. If M is the household’s nominal cash reserve, matching its target means M/P=L. This is a household budget/portfolio consistency condition, not aggregate money-market clearing. The household does not determine economy-wide prices, monetary policy or market interest rates.

Initially it holds M=1160 and exactly meets its real reserve target. A price inferred from M/L is the consumption-price index consistent with that target; a higher threshold does not predict an actual price jump. All price, return and income alternatives are supplied or inferred conditionally as the question specifies.

A separate certain zero-coupon bond is bought for 100 and pays a fixed nominal 106 at maturity. The household may need to sell it early to pay an upfront separate-living bill. For its realized real return, use exact inflation adjustment rather than the approximate anticipated relation in the cash-demand model.

The stated inflation forecasts, quoted yields and cash-access conditions are hypothetical terms facing this household, not consequences attributed to the public acknowledgement. No actual relationship, private financial event or market response is asserted.
objectives: Calculate how upfront household expenses and nominal returns affect a desired cash reserve.
Distinguish an inferred cash-target price threshold from a causal price forecast.
Compare selling a fixed-payoff bond before maturity with holding it for a later bill.
cases.focus: Cash targets, fixed-payoff bonds and the purchasing power of a household’s transition budget

cases.title: Tracking the affair-counselling service cycle

A fictional network of counselling services works with households after affair disclosures. Managers use quarterly appointment activity, equipment investment and a survey of workers offering these services to plan capacity. These are the network’s own service-sector indicators, not counts of affairs and not evidence of an economy-wide recession.

Its real appointment-service activity index Y at quarters t=0,…,8 is [100,102,105,103,101,104,108,107,109]. An increase represents more delivered services, not necessarily more underlying affairs. Access, referrals, capacity and repeat appointments can also affect activity.

The baseline planning trend is Tₜ=100+t. Unless changed, the absolute service-cycle gap is Yₜ−Tₜ. A strict interior peak exceeds both adjacent observations; a strict trough is below both. Endpoints do not establish turning points.

The network’s nominal cash-reserve stock at t=0,…,8 is [200,204,214,230,235,238,250,270,275]. Quarter-t reserve growth is 100(Mₜ/Mₜ₋₁−1). These are private balances held to pay staff and bills, not the national money supply. Compare corresponding turns in growth, not in the rising stock.

A survey’s unemployment rate among workers offering these services at t=0,…,8 is [6,5.5,5,5.2,6,5.5,4.8,5,4.6]. Use the usual employed-plus-unemployed denominator for this defined surveyed labor force. A part separately supplies an equipment-investment index or the service-price index.

Each part uses the original data unless it explicitly supplies revised appointment records or another planning trend. Course cycle concepts are applied descriptively to this sector. No date is mapped to actual Huang news, and no personal event is assumed to move GDP or national employment.
objectives: Use service activity and stock-growth measures for the appropriate planning comparison.
Distinguish the network’s real activity, cash revenue, trend position and labor-market indicator.
Reassess capacity-planning conclusions when records or trend assumptions change.

cases.title: A midterm infrastructure pledge and its financing
cases.context: US midterms elect representatives to both chambers of Congress.

A hypothetical congressional platform proposes additional public infrastructure purchases. G records purchases actually delivered, and T records current lump-sum taxes actually collected. Alternative enacted versions use debt finance, current taxation or spending cuts. The Federal Reserve independently chooses M; a candidate cannot promise its cooperation. Every coordinated outcome below is conditional on the Fed making the specified separate decision. Use a closed economy with C=20+0.6(Y−T)−2r, I=30−3r, Y=C+I+G and real money demand L=Y−10r. T is a lump-sum tax. Consumption responds to current taxes as written, without Ricardian offset.

Each part is a separate experiment from the stated baseline unless it explicitly supplies a different starting point. Changes in G do not directly shift labor supply or technology in this exercise.
objectives: Derive equilibrium from spending and portfolio choices
Separate direct fiscal demand from financing and induced responses
Find instrument combinations for output, consumption and investment targets

A hypothetical congressional relief platform is evaluated while the nominal rate is at its lower bound. Each part resets to the baseline unless it explicitly supplies another expectation or target. The piecewise rule must be checked after solving, and none of these policies is asserted to have actually occurred.

Verify which branch of LM supports a proposed equilibrium
Identify policy targets that require changing expectations or spending

cases.title: Does a tax-financed jobs platform change capacity?

A hypothetical tax-financed purchase proposal is represented by two stated reduced-form shifts, supply changing to Nˢ=2w+2 and a rising to 32. Other parts specify separate resets. These are illustrative assumptions rather than a universal quantified fiscal response.

A hypothetical midterm platform seeks demand support and claims that monetary accommodation can preserve additional jobs. Congress determines the stipulated enacted net-purchase change in a, while every change in M is a separate, independent Fed decision. Most parts hold fiscal implementation at baseline to isolate the requested monetary channel; the final part allows both institutions to act. Producers choose output using expected general prices. Whether the Fed communicates before or after those choices is therefore central to the platform’s claimed employment effect.

The hypothetical economy has surprise supply Y=100+25(P−Pᵉ), with price levels rather than log prices in this equation. Goods equilibrium is r=a−0.08Y and real money demand is L=Y−5r. Rates and a use percentage-point units.
Initially a=14,M=140 and P=Pᵉ=2. Real capacity remains Y*=100. In an unexpected experiment, Pᵉ initially stays at its pre-announcement value. With fully correct expectations, P=Pᵉ and Y=100.

Each part resets to this baseline unless it supplies a different observation. M/P=L must hold together with goods and supply equations. Fully anticipated policy changes are credible and known before production decisions.
objectives: Solve the interaction of demand and price surprises
Separate anticipated policy from delayed expectation correction
Use observed outcomes to infer hidden expectations and offsetting shocks
cases.focus: Institutional separation, announcement timing and offsetting implementation shocks

cases.title: Procurement promises meet effort and staffing rules
cases.context: US midterms elect representatives to both chambers of Congress.
scenario: Every platform, legislative outcome, policy choice, numerical value and economic response below is hypothetical. No actual election winner, enacted law or measured US effect is asserted. A campaign promise alone changes no current instrument unless a part explicitly supplies an expectations channel.

A hypothetical midterm procurement platform is evaluated at one small contractor, not as aggregate US GDP. Its funded worksite equipment and infrastructure can change the specified productivity coefficient A, while contract wage clauses, approved pay bands and staffing authorizations change feasible choices. Larger public demand alone is not interpreted as greater technical productivity. The output price and effort schedule remain as stated. Each institutional change takes effect only in the part that explicitly imposes it; pending campaign promises leave the contractor’s baseline choices unchanged.

A hypothetical contractor can pay a real wage w>0. Effort is e(w)=w²/(9+w²), effective labor is E=e(w)N, output is Y=24A√E, and operating profit is Y−wN. Workers are divisible and output is sold at a normalized real price of one.
Initially A=1 and enough workers are available. Except for explicitly stated restrictions, both wage and headcount can be chosen. The no-operation choice has zero operating profit.

Some parts separately impose a wage floor, a headcount cap or a discrete wage set. A final part stipulates a fixed administrative cost of resetting nominal pay, using the same net-gain logic as the lecture’s reset-cost comparison. These restrictions are original teaching assumptions.
objectives: Derive the optimal effort-adjusted wage and actual headcount
Check when wage or labor constraints replace the interior conditions
Compare the value of changing pay after a nominal price shock
cases.focus: Implemented contract rules, productive public inputs and the cost of pay adjustment

cases.title: Public orders, contract standards and posted prices
cases.context: US midterms elect representatives to both chambers of Congress.
scenario: Every platform, legislative outcome, policy choice, numerical value and economic response below is hypothetical. No actual election winner, enacted law or measured US effect is asserted. A campaign promise alone changes no current instrument unless a part explicitly supplies an expectations channel.

A small supplier sells into a market that includes public buyers. A hypothetical midterm procurement platform changes actual orders only when its budgets are implemented. Larger or cancelled order authorizations shift the demand intercept a, while new required material standards can change marginal cost c. Revising catalogues and order systems incurs F. These are firm-level demand and cost experiments, not changes in an aggregate price index or claims about national output. Each part names the enacted change; mere campaign rhetoric does not change the supplier’s orders.

A hypothetical supplier faces orders Q=max((a−P)/0.5,0), where P is its selling price. It has constant real marginal cost c, no fixed operating cost and enough production capacity. At any posted price it may sell the demanded amount or choose zero production.
Initially a=20,c=4 and the posted price is P=12. Resetting its price costs F=18 once; keeping its old price or producing nothing incurs no reset cost. A reset can choose any nonnegative price.

If net profits tie, the manager retains the old price. Each part is a separate experiment unless it specifies otherwise. The demand and cost changes are hypothetical responses to possible policy conditions, not measured US effects.
objectives: Distinguish frictionless markup from a profitable price reset
Compare positive and negative shocks when the zero-orders boundary matters
Infer adjustment-cost thresholds from observed decisions

cases.title: Midterm employment promises and moving inflation trade-offs
cases.context: US midterms elect representatives to both chambers of Congress.

Hypothetical congressional platforms promise demand support, spending restraint or structural employment measures. Enacted demand changes affect actual unemployment only through the stated scenario outcomes; the Phillips relation does not itself specify a fiscal multiplier. Supply measures or implementation failures change the natural rate, potential output or response coefficient only when explicitly given. The Fed’s policy response and households’ inflation forecasts are separate from congressional promises. These conditional calculations assess whether the platforms’ employment and inflation claims can coexist, without selecting parties or asserting election results.

Use p=ln(P). Inflation π is measured in 100 log-point units, and unemployment u is in percentage points. Initially Y*=100,u*=5 and Y−Y*=1000(p−pᵉ). The output-unemployment relation is Y−Y*=−4(u−u*). Expected inflation is initially 2.

Actual and expected inflation share the same previous-price baseline, so π−πᵉ=100(p−pᵉ). Demand policy can change actual unemployment, while a supply or structural change may change Y*,u* or the price-surprise coefficient only when explicitly stated.

Each part resets to the baseline unless it explicitly supplies new parameters. Probability distributions, persistence rules and uncertainty intervals are original hypothetical illustrations. They are not estimated US relationships or guaranteed policy effects.
objectives: Derive the Phillips coefficient with consistent units
Distinguish changed expectations, actual outcomes and natural benchmarks
Solve inverse and robust targets while respecting expectation adjustment

questions.prompt: The affair-disclosure desk has subscribers ready to buy its verified summaries. At baseline A=4, K=25, P=1, W=5, it must choose paid verification hours before publishing. Which profit-maximizing (N, Y, wN) should its staffing plan use?

choices.feedback: For positive A and K, marginal product is arbitrarily high near zero; some hiring is profitable.
MPN=10/√N equals 5 at N=4; production and the wage bill then follow.
This halves the correct employment; MPN at N=2 still exceeds the wage.
The wage bill is wN=5×4, not total output.
This sets average product, rather than marginal product, equal to the wage.
Installed capital need not equal employment, and marginal profit is negative at this employment.

questions.explanation: Y=20√N, so real operating surplus is 20√N−5N. Its derivative 10/√N−5 is zero at √N=2, and its second derivative is negative. Thus N=4, Y=40 and wN=20. This surplus is before capital payment. For this desk, the labor bill pays verification staff; the remaining 20 output units are the return before capital costs, not evidence of pure profit from the disclosure.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: Reset the reporting desk to baseline. A new public-statement matching workflow raises A from 4 to 5 without changing archive equipment K=25, client price P=1 or real hourly wage w=5. If subscribers buy the extra summaries and the desk reoptimizes hiring, which N and percentage output gain result?

choices.feedback: The new output is 62.5; its gain relative to 40 is 22.5/40.

choices.text: N=3.2; Y is unchanged.
choices.feedback: A productivity rise raises labor demand at a fixed real wage.
The productivity gain raises output directly and induces hiring, so output rises more than 25%.

choices.text: N=4; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: This holds employment fixed even though the firm is allowed to reoptimize.

choices.text: N=5; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: Employment scales with A squared in this demand function, not linearly.

choices.text: N=6.25; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: This gets hiring right but omits the induced-employment output gain.

questions.explanation: MPN=12.5/√N=5 gives √N=2.5 and N=6.25. Output becomes 5√(25×6.25)=62.5. The increase is (62.5−40)/40=0.5625. The old labor-demand schedule has shifted, not merely been traversed. The workflow change expands summary production directly and makes additional verification hours worthwhile; counting only the 25% direct improvement understates the staffing response.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: Reset to baseline. Demand for affair-disclosure verification leads competing desks to bid up the real hourly wage from 5 to 6.25. At the same time this desk adopts the workflow that raises A from 4 to 5. K stays 25 and all summaries can be sold. Which employment and output comparison should the desk report?

choices.text: N falls to 2.56 and Y to 40.
choices.feedback: That is the wage-only hiring response evaluated while overlooking the productivity gain.

choices.text: N stays 4 and Y rises to 62.5.
choices.feedback: At N=4, the production function gives 5√100=50.

choices.text: N rises 25% and Y rises 50%.
choices.feedback: Employment depends on the ratio A/w squared; that ratio has not changed.

choices.text: N stays 4 and Y rises to 50: A/w is unchanged, but technology still raises output at that employment.
choices.feedback: Offsetting hiring incentives do not imply that production itself stays unchanged.

choices.text: N and Y both stay unchanged.
choices.feedback: Constant A/w preserves the hiring optimum, not the productivity multiplier in Y.

choices.text: N rises to 6.25 and Y to 62.5.
choices.feedback: That is the A-only experiment and ignores the higher wage.

questions.explanation: N=K[A/(2w)]². The old ratio 4/10 and new ratio 5/12.5 are both 0.4, giving N=25×0.16=4. Y nevertheless changes from 4√100 to 5√100=50. Real labor income rises from 20 to 25 and remains half of output. Here the higher productivity and the competing wage offer preserve A/w, so paid hours stay at 4 even though completed summaries rise from 40 to 50. Constant hours do not mean the workflow had no effect.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: Reset A=4, K=25. Publishers’ stipulated willingness to pay for verified affair summaries raises their price P from 1 to 1.5, while competition for staff raises nominal W from 5 to 6. What output-unit labor cost w, real summary output Y and nominal sales PY should the desk budget?

choices.feedback: Divide the nominal hourly wage by the summary selling price. The ratio measures the desk’s labor cost in output units; multiplying W and P does not.

choices.text: w=4, Y=40 and PY=60.
choices.feedback: The real wage is right, but employment must be reoptimized.
This labels nominal revenue as real output and multiplies by P twice.

choices.text: w=5, Y=40 and PY=60.
choices.feedback: A nominal change is not neutral when the nominal wage and output price grow by different proportions.

choices.text: w=4, Y=50 and PY=75.
choices.feedback: The nominal wage rises less than prices; the lower real hiring cost increases labor and real output.
This treats the nominal wage as the real wage despite the price change.

questions.explanation: w=6/1.5=4. Then 10/√N=4 implies N=6.25. Real production is 20√6.25=50 and nominal revenue is 1.5×50=75. The calculation compares the wage and selling price before solving the real decision. Staff receive more money per hour, but each hour costs fewer summary output units because the client price rises faster. This is the desk’s own output price, not a claim about economy-wide inflation or workers’ consumption purchasing power.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations. Real/nominal distinction: Lecture 1, model and measurement definitions.

questions.prompt: Equipment-planning reset: the reporting desk starts with archive/editing capital K=25. Twenty percent wears out during the period, and the desk installs 9 gross units to maintain capacity for affair-disclosure verification. Next period A=4 and N=4 are fixed. Which next capital stock K′, net investment and next-period MPN are correct?

choices.text: K′=34, net investment=9, MPN=√34.
choices.feedback: This ignores depreciation of the installed stock.

choices.text: K′=20, net investment=−5, MPN=√20.
choices.feedback: This includes depreciation but omits the new investment.

choices.text: K′=29, net investment=9, MPN=√29.
choices.feedback: The capital stock is right, but net investment subtracts depreciation.

choices.text: K′=29, net investment=4, MPN=2√29.
choices.feedback: MPN=(A/2)√(K/N); with A=4 and N=4 the coefficient becomes one.

choices.text: K′=30.8, net investment=5.8, MPN=√30.8.
choices.feedback: The specified rule depreciates 25 initial units by 20%, leaving 20, then adds all 9 new units: K′=29. The proposed 30.8 does not satisfy that accumulation rule.

choices.text: K′=29, net investment=4, and MPN=√29.
choices.feedback: Replacement uses 5 investment units; the remaining 4 expand capital and raise labor productivity.

questions.explanation: K′=(1−0.2)25+9=29. Net investment is K′−K=4=9−5. At fixed N=4, MPN=(4/2)√(29/4)=√29, compared with baseline MPN=5. This is a fixed-employment marginal-product comparison, not the new hiring equilibrium. The nine installed units are a flow; only four expand the desk’s usable archive beyond its original stock after replacing wear. The resulting marginal product refers to verification labor using that next-period equipment.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations. Capital stock-flow identity: Lecture 1, stocks and flows; Lecture 3 part 3, gross investment and depreciation.

questions.prompt: Capacity-plan reset: a publisher commits to buy 80 verified affair-summary units. Before choosing labor, the desk can select installed K; take A=4 and real hourly wage w=5. Find a capacity-and-hours pair that produces exactly 80 and also satisfies its subsequent hiring condition MPN=w. This is a capacity consistency calculation, not a capital-profit optimum without a capital price. Which pair and output-per-hour comparison are correct?

choices.text: (K,N)=(50,8); output per paid verification hour stays 10.
choices.feedback: The unchanged real wage fixes K/N; doubling output therefore doubles both inputs.

choices.text: (25,16); output per paid verification hour falls to 5.
choices.feedback: This produces 80, but MPN is 2.5, below the wage; the labor choice is not optimal.

choices.text: (100,4); output per paid verification hour rises to 20.
choices.feedback: This produces 80, but MPN is 10, above the wage; the firm wants more workers.

choices.text: (50,4); output per paid verification hour is 20.
choices.feedback: Output with those inputs is 40√2, not 80.

choices.text: (100,16); output per paid verification hour stays 10.
choices.feedback: Those inputs produce 160, twice the requested target.

choices.text: (25,8); output per paid verification hour stays 10.
choices.feedback: These inputs neither produce 80 nor satisfy MPN=5.

questions.explanation: For this square-root function, wN=Y/2 when MPN=w. Thus N=80/(2×5)=8. Then 80=4√(8K) gives K=50. Both inputs double from (25, 4), so constant returns doubles output and leaves Y/N=10 unchanged. Doubling the contracted summary volume requires doubling both archive capacity and verification hours along this fixed-wage expansion path. Holding K=25 and merely doubling output would violate the labor hiring condition.

questions.prompt: Payment-audit reset: a fictional affair verification desk uses K=36, N=9 and pays real wage w=6. Both labor and archive capital receive their marginal products under Y=A√(KN). Infer A, Y, MPK and pure economic profit so the desk can distinguish capital compensation from profit. Which report is consistent?

choices.text: A=6, Y=108, MPK=6 and pure profit=0.
choices.feedback: Equal factor shares do not imply equal per-unit factor prices when K and N differ.

choices.text: A=6, Y=108, MPK=1.5 and pure profit=0.
choices.feedback: The wage equation identifies A; both factor bills then exhaust output.

choices.text: A=3, Y=54, MPK=.75 and pure profit=0.
choices.feedback: At A=3, MPN would be 3, contradicting the observed wage 6.

choices.text: A=6, Y=108, MPK=3 and pure profit=−54.
choices.feedback: MPK has coefficient A/2; the stated rental doubles the marginal capital product.

choices.text: A=6, Y=108, MPK=1.5 and pure profit=54.
choices.feedback: 54 is the residual after labor alone; paying capital removes it.

choices.text: A=12, Y=216, MPK=3 and pure profit=54.
choices.feedback: This misses the one-half coefficient when inferring A from MPN.

questions.explanation: MPN=(A/2)√(36/9)=A, so A=6. Y=6√324=108. MPK=(6/2)√(9/36)=1.5. Labor is paid 6×9=54 and capital 1.5×36=54. Pure profit after both payments is 108−54−54=0; the labor-only residual is capital income. The 54 left after verification wages is the archive owners’ factor income. Once those owners are paid MPK×K=54, pure profit is zero; the service’s revenue is not all a windfall for its operator.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: Temporary-desk decision: reset A=4, K=25, w=5. Only 3 trained verification hours are available for this edition’s affair disclosures, so N≤3. Archive capital is already sunk, but opening the edition requires an avoidable editorial/verification setup cost F≥0 in output units. Closing yields zero. What exact F range makes opening strictly better, and should the desk open at F=20?

choices.text: Operate for every F because MPN exceeds w at N=3.
choices.feedback: Positive marginal profit at the staffing ceiling does not guarantee positive total operating profit after F.

choices.text: Operate if F≤20√3−15; the endpoint is strictly preferable to shutdown.
choices.feedback: At equality operating profit is zero, so there is indifference rather than strict preference.

choices.text: Operate strictly rather than shut down only if F<20√3−15≈19.641; at F=20, shut down.
choices.feedback: The capacity binds before MPN reaches the wage, so the best operating surplus must be evaluated at N=3.

choices.text: Operate if F<20; at F=20 it is indifferent.
choices.feedback: 20 is the unconstrained maximum surplus at N=4; that employment is unavailable.

choices.text: Operate if F<15; at F=20 shut down.
choices.feedback: 15 is the wage bill, not revenue minus variable costs.

choices.text: Operate if F<20√3; at F=20 operate.
choices.feedback: This compares fixed cost with revenue without paying workers.

questions.explanation: Operating surplus before F is g(N)=20√N−5N. Over 0<N≤3, g′(N)=10/√N−5>0, so the constrained operating choice is N=3. Its surplus is 20√3−15≈19.641. Subtract F and compare with zero. F below this threshold gives strict operation, equality gives indifference, and F=20 makes shutdown better. The marginal hiring condition and the total participation comparison are separate. Even though another trained hour would be productive, it is unavailable. Opening therefore depends on the surplus from the three feasible hours covering the avoidable setup cost; positive marginal product alone cannot justify this edition.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations. First-order versus boundary maximization: Lecture 1, optimization review.

questions.prompt: Baseline recovery-time plan: the adult can accept counselling-centre administrative work at w=3, has a work-independent support grant m=18 and h=12 discretionary hours. With nonwork recovery time l horizontal and ordinary consumption c vertical, which budget description correctly separates available choices from an impossible extension of the line?

choices.text: The slope is −1/3 and the vertical intercept is 54.
choices.feedback: With consumption vertical the slope is −w, not its reciprocal.

choices.text: The feasible boundary joins (0,18) to (12,54).
choices.feedback: This reverses the earnings effect of leisure.

choices.text: Only the point (12,18) is feasible.
choices.feedback: Positive work also finances consumption; this point is just the no-work endpoint.

choices.text: The budget line slopes −3, approaches (0,54), and reaches the no-work point (12,18); its extended horizontal intercept 18 is infeasible.
choices.feedback: The positive-leisure domain excludes l=0 itself, while l=12 is allowed. The time endowment rules out the extended intercept l=18.

choices.text: The feasible boundary joins (0,36) to (12,0).
choices.feedback: Both endpoints omit the 18 units of nonlabor income.

choices.text: The entire line through (0,54) and (18,0) is feasible.
choices.feedback: Leisure between 12 and 18 violates the time endowment.

questions.explanation: The budget boundary is c=3(12−l)+18=54−3l for 0<l≤12. As l approaches zero, consumption approaches 54, but l=0 itself is excluded by the stated logarithmic-utility domain. The allowed no-work endpoint is (12, 18). Extending the line to c=0 gives l=18, which violates the time endowment and is not a feasible choice. The support grant finances 18 consumption units even if the adult takes all 12 hours for nonwork recovery. It does not create extra hours; the apparent intercept at 18 hours is unavailable.
questions.source: Tutorial 2 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 2 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original numerical application of the consumption-leisure budget and wage decomposition.

questions.prompt: Reset the support grant to m=18 and h=12. A stipulated rise in counselling caseload makes the centre offer w=6 for administrative hours, leaving the adult’s U=ln c+2ln l unchanged. What optimal (nonwork time l, paid hours N, consumption c) should they choose?

choices.feedback: At the no-work point, the wage exceeds the willingness to trade leisure for consumption; working is beneficial.
This assigns only half the correct leisure; the utility weight on leisure is 2.
Consumption includes 18 nonlabor income as well as 12 earnings.
This violates the time ceiling and the positive-consumption domain.
Tangency gives 2c/l=6, and the resulting leisure lies below the time ceiling.
Equal time in work and leisure ignores both the utility weight and nonlabor income.

questions.explanation: Substituting the budget gives ln(90−6l)+2ln l. Its derivative is −6/c+2/l=0, hence c=3l. Combining with c=90−6l gives l=10, N=2 and c=30. Strict concavity and feasibility make this the unique optimum. At this offer the adult accepts two administrative hours and keeps ten hours for nonwork recovery. The grant remains available, so consumption includes both earnings and support.
questions.source: Tutorial 2 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 2 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original numerical application of the consumption-leisure budget and wage decomposition.

questions.prompt: Start from the w=6, m=18 recovery plan (l, N, c)=(10, 2, 30). An assistance arrangement raises the adult’s work-independent grant to 36 while the centre’s wage stays 6. What is the new optimum, and what happens if the grant rises slightly above 36?

choices.text: At m=36, N=−2; above it, work becomes still more negative.
choices.feedback: A formula extended beyond l=12 is infeasible.

choices.text: At m=36, (l,N,c)=(10,2,48), and leisure stays fixed.
choices.feedback: This ignores the income effect on normal leisure.
At zero work consumption equals m=36, not full income wh+m.

choices.text: At m=36, work rises to 4 because consumption is normal.
choices.feedback: Normal leisure reduces work when nonlabor income rises.

choices.text: The optimum reaches zero work only at m=72.
choices.feedback: The leisure weight is 2, so its no-work threshold is wh/2, not wh.

choices.text: At m=36, (l,N,c)=(12,0,36); above 36, N remains 0 and additional income raises c.
choices.feedback: The unconstrained leisure choice reaches the time limit at 36, then the no-work corner prevents further leisure increases.

questions.explanation: Interior leisure is l=2(wh+m)/(3w). At w=6 this equals 8+m/9, reaching 12 when m=36. For m>36 the interior candidate exceeds 12, so the constraint binds at l=12. Consumption is then m and work remains zero; negative work is never available. The grant allows the adult to stop paid administrative work at 36. Further support can raise consumption but cannot create more than the available 12 nonwork hours; applying the interior formula beyond that point would invent negative work.
questions.source: Tutorial 2 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 2 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original numerical application of the consumption-leisure budget and wage decomposition.

questions.prompt: Reset to m=18 and the centre’s wage w=6. Greater demand for counselling administration raises its offer to 12. The adult’s old (l, c) is (10, 30), and actual new choice is (9, 54). To isolate the incentive to give up recovery time, use Hicks compensation at the old model utility; set a=∛500≈7.937. Which work decomposition is correct?

choices.text: Substitution raises work by 10−a≈2.063; income lowers it by 9−a≈1.063; total work rises by 1.
choices.feedback: The compensated point has leisure a, while actual leisure rises from a to 9 after restoring purchasing power.

choices.text: Substitution raises work by 1 and income has no effect.
choices.feedback: The actual change alone does not identify the two compensated components.

choices.text: Substitution lowers work by 2.063 and income raises it by 1.063.
choices.feedback: Both signs are reversed: leisure is more expensive, while the income effect favors leisure.

choices.text: Both substitution and income raise work, totaling 3.126.
choices.feedback: Normal leisure makes the income effect reduce work.

choices.text: Substitution raises work by 2 and income lowers it by 1 exactly.
choices.feedback: The compensated leisure is a cube root, not 8.

choices.text: Income lowers work by 2.063, so total work falls by 1.
choices.feedback: The component magnitudes have been swapped; the actual optimum supplies one more hour.

questions.explanation: The old utility is equivalent to c l²=30×10²=3000. At the new wage, tangency is 2c/l=12, so c=6l. Holding old utility gives 6l³=3000 and l=a. Work moves from 2 to 12−a, then to 3. Hence the changes are 10−a and a−9, summing to 1. The compensation holds utility, not income, fixed. The higher offered wage makes an hour away from paid counselling administration more costly, raising compensated work. The extra purchasing power then restores some nonwork recovery time, leaving only one additional paid hour overall.
questions.source: Tutorial 2 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 2 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original numerical application of the consumption-leisure budget and wage decomposition.

questions.prompt: Participation-planning reset: the adult retains the grant m=18 and original preferences. The counselling centre may offer any w>0 for administrative shifts, with h=12. Which complete hours rule tells the centre when this adult accepts paid shifts and when the adult instead uses all available time for nonwork recovery?

choices.text: N(w)=4 for every wage because logarithmic utility eliminates income effects.
choices.feedback: Nonlabor income makes the actual wage response nonzero; logarithmic utility does not eliminate its income component.

choices.text: N(w)=max{0,4−12/w}; work starts only when w>3.
choices.feedback: The interior formula must be truncated at zero work; at w=3 the unconstrained choice just reaches the endpoint.

choices.text: N(w)=4−12/w for every w>0, including negative work below 3.
choices.feedback: Negative work would require leisure above the 12-hour time endowment, so the unconstrained formula must be truncated.

choices.text: N(w)=max{0,12−12/w}; work starts above 1.
choices.feedback: This omits the two-thirds allocation of full income to leisure.

choices.text: N(w)=4+12/w; work always falls when w rises.
choices.feedback: The nonlabor-income term reduces work, so it enters with a minus sign.

choices.text: N(w)=0 for w≤6 and 4−12/w above 6.
choices.feedback: The no-work threshold is 3; at w=6 work is already 2.

questions.explanation: The interior solution is l=2(12w+18)/(3w)=8+12/w, giving N=4−12/w. It is feasible only when N≥0, equivalent to w≥3. For w<3, leisure is capped at 12. On the interior branch, dN/dw=12/w²>0; below the threshold the response is zero. The rule is continuous but kinked at 3. The centre gets no hours from this adult at offers up to 3.
